title: E-Discovery and Large-Scale Document Analysis
answer: Predictive coding, cross-lingual review, audio and video evidence, privilege logging, and sentiment analysis of corporate messaging.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
children.blurb: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review cover the use of machine learning to rank or classify large document sets for litigation and investigation, most often to separate responsive material from the rest before a review team sees it.

children.name: Cross-Lingual Discovery
children.blurb: Cross-lingual discovery is the practice of finding and producing relevant material in a legal matter when the documents, chats, and audio are not all in one language.

children.name: Audio and Video Evidence
children.blurb: Audio and video evidence covers recorded speech, surveillance footage, body camera video, call recordings, voicemail, and meeting captures that become part of a legal matter.

children.name: Automated Privilege Logging
children.blurb: Automated privilege logging is the use of software to identify, describe and list documents withheld from production in litigation because they are protected by attorney client privilege or the work product doctrine.

children.name: Intent and Sentiment in Corporate Communications
children.blurb: Intent and sentiment analysis in corporate communications covers the automated reading of emails, chat logs, memos, and filings to infer what a writer meant and how they felt.

sections.body: E-discovery is the process of finding, reviewing, and producing documents and other material when organizations are involved in litigation, investigations, or regulatory requests. In practice, artificial intelligence does the heavy lifting of sorting through millions of emails, chat logs, contracts, and recordings so that human reviewers see a smaller, ranked set first. Predictive coding, also called technology-assisted review, trains a model on decisions reviewers have already made and then scores the remaining documents for relevance. Cross-lingual tools translate and classify material written in many languages within one workflow, and audio and video analysis turns speech into searchable text. Privilege logging uses classifiers to flag attorney-client material, and sentiment analysis reads corporate messaging for tone and intent. None of this replaces legal judgment, it changes where human attention goes.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Predictive coding is the most mature part of this field and is accepted in several jurisdictions, though courts and opposing parties still argue over how transparent a model must be and how its recall should be validated. Cross-lingual review works well for major languages and degrades on low-resource ones, idioms, and mixed-script text. Audio and video evidence has become practical because transcription quality improved, but speaker identification, overlapping speech, and poor recordings remain hard. Automated privilege logging produces useful first drafts and still generates false positives and false negatives that reviewers must catch, since a missed privileged document can waive protection. Sentiment and intent models are the least settled, because tone in corporate writing is subtle and a flagged message is not proof of anything. The honest limit across all of it is that these systems rank and organize, they do not decide, and their errors are unevenly distributed across languages and writing styles.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the pipeline of a modern review. Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review is the anchor, covering how relevance models are trained, tested, and defended, and a reader goes there for the core method. Cross-Lingual Discovery extends that method to multilingual material and is the place to look when a matter spans several languages. Audio and Video Evidence covers the conversion of speech and recordings into reviewable text and the problems that come with it. Automated Privilege Logging addresses the separate task of identifying protected material and building the log itself. Intent and Sentiment in Corporate Communications sits at the interpretive end, dealing with what tone and phrasing in messages may suggest and why that reading is contested. Read together they show one workflow from collection to interpretation, and read separately each answers a specific question a review team will face.
